A satchel is a type of bag designed to be carried over one shoulder. Its most recognizable feature is a flap — a wide fold of material that comes down over the opening of the bag and fastens shut, usually with a buckle or clasp. Think of it like a big envelope that you wear.

A satchel has a few defining physical traits:

  • A structured, rectangular shape — it holds its form well and can usually stand upright on its own, unlike a soft, floppy bag.
  • A large flap on top that folds over the front of the bag and closes it. This flap is the satchel's most iconic design element.
  • A long shoulder strap — this is how you carry it. You loop it over one shoulder so the bag rests at your hip or side. Some satchels also have a short handle at the top for carrying by hand.
  • One or more roomy compartments inside, big enough for books, files, a laptop, or similar items.

Traditionally, satchels were made of leather, which gave them a sturdy, slightly formal look. Today, they also come in canvas, nylon, and synthetic materials, so they can look casual or professional depending on the design.

The satchel is a practical, everyday bag. Its main purpose is to carry things you need throughout the day — especially flat, organized items like:

  • Books and notebooks
  • Documents and files
  • A laptop or tablet
  • Stationery, a wallet, keys, and other essentials

It sits in that sweet spot between "too small to be useful" and "too large to be practical for daily life." It's bigger than a handbag but smaller than a travel bag.

Historically, satchels were the classic school bag. Children would carry their books to school in a leather satchel slung over one shoulder — this image is so common that in many people's minds, the word "satchel" immediately brings up a schoolchild. This association is especially strong in British culture.

Today, satchels are used by all kinds of people:

  • Students carrying textbooks and stationery
  • Professionals carrying documents, a laptop, or work materials
  • Everyday people who want a stylish, organized bag for going about their day

You wear a satchel on one shoulder, with the bag hanging at your side or in front of your hip. This is different from a backpack, which rests on your back using both shoulders. Because the weight sits on one side of your body, some people switch shoulders occasionally for comfort.
How a Satchel Differs from Similar Bags

Understanding what a satchel is not helps sharpen your picture of it:

Satchel vs. Backpack: A backpack goes on your back and uses two shoulder straps. A satchel uses one long strap and hangs at your side. Backpacks tend to feel more casual or sporty; satchels feel slightly more polished.

Satchel vs. Briefcase: A briefcase is rigid and boxy, carried by a short handle, and associated with formal business settings. A satchel has a softer structure, a shoulder strap, and a flap closure — it's more versatile and less strictly formal.

Satchel vs. Tote Bag: A tote bag has an open top (no flap or zipper to close it), is usually softer and more casual, and has two short handles rather than a long shoulder strap. A satchel is more structured, has that signature flap, and is designed to be worn on the shoulder.

Satchel vs. Messenger Bag: These two are closely related and are sometimes used interchangeably. The key distinction is that a satchel specifically features that flap-and-buckle closure and a more structured body. A messenger bag is a broader category — it also goes over one shoulder, but may have a zipper, velcro, or other closures and tends to have a flatter, less structured profile.
The Vibe and Feel of the Word

When people use the word "satchel," there's often a slight classic, timeless, or academic quality to what they're imagining — a worn leather bag on a professor, a schoolchild's shoulder bag, or a journalist's field bag. It's not a trendy, flashy word. It carries a sense of practicality mixed with a bit of old-school charm.

• She packed her textbooks into her satchel and headed to class.
  • He unbuckled the flap of his leather satchel and pulled out a stack of documents.
  • The old professor always arrived with a battered satchel hanging from his shoulder.
  • She slung the satchel across her body and walked out the door.
  • The satchel was deep enough to hold a laptop, a notebook, and a water bottle.

A satchel is a structured, shoulder-carry bag with a distinctive flap closure, used to carry books, documents, or everyday essentials. It is defined by its shape (rectangular, can stand on its own), its closure (a flap that folds over the top and buckles or clasps shut), and how it's carried (over one shoulder on a long strap). It sits in a middle ground — more organized than a tote, more casual than a briefcase, and more stylish than a plain backpack.
